papers.title: Simple, accurate lumped-element models of distributed resonators for superconducting quantum circuits
papers.abstract: Superconducting quantum circuit design is reliant on accurately mapping design parameters to a quantum Hamiltonian. Designers typically rely on computationally intensive finite-element electromagnetic simulations. However, effective circuit-level models can in principle capture much of the relevant physics for these systems, reducing the need for finite-element simulations. A barrier to implementing these simpler models has been the prevalence of distributed elements such as coplanar waveguides resonators in device designs. Techniques for modeling these distributed elements have been developed, but may be difficult to scale, reduce intuition, and give inaccurate results under strong coupling. In this work we describe a simple effective circuit-level model that faithfully reproduces the scattering parameters, and subsequently can predict certain Hamiltonian parameters, for a coupled, distributed element within a broader two-port network even up to strong coupling. Our approach does not explicitly require an electromagnetic simulation. Our model, along with other common lumped models used in black box quantization, is publicly available to researchers via an open-source code package, $\texttt{simpleLOMs}$.

summary.summary: This work presents a method to replace distributed transmission line resonators in superconducting circuits with accurate single parallel $LC$ lumped elements by fitting scattering parameters in the presence of coupling capacitors. The technique outperforms traditional analytical lumped oscillator models and Foster synthesis approaches, particularly under heavy loading, and is implemented in the open-source package $\texttt{simpleLOMs}$.
summary.motivation: Superconducting circuit designers need computationally tractable lumped-element models for quantization, but existing approaches for modeling loaded distributed resonators (such as coupled CPW resonators) become inaccurate under strong coupling or require cumbersome phenomenological adjustments.
summary.method: The authors fit effective $C_\mathrm{eff}$ and $L_\mathrm{eff}$ values of a single $LC$ circuit to match the scattering parameters ($S_{11}$ and $S_{22}$) of a transmission line with its coupling capacitors explicitly included, using least-squares regression in the frequency range $f_0 \pm 5\kappa$ and validating against ANSYS HFSS simulations.
summary.result: The optimized model predicts shifted resonant frequencies and linewidths of coupled CPW resonators with errors below 0.5% and 3% respectively across coupling capacitances up to 200 fF, outperforming both analytical models and Foster synthesis methods which produced significantly larger errors especially at high coupling strengths.

papers.title: Biased-noise qubits: a guide to efficient fault-tolerance using the hierarchy of errors
papers.abstract: Qubits with strongly biased noise, in which phase-flip errors are orders of magnitude more frequent than bit-flips, arise both naturally, as in electron and nuclear spins, and by engineering, as in stabilized cat qubits. This noise structure holds the promise of reducing the daunting hardware overhead of fault-tolerant quantum computing, but exploiting it requires physical operations that do not convert frequent phase-flips into rare bit-flips. In this review, we analyze the most prominent fault-tolerant protocols for biased-noise qubits, organized according to the available set of such bias-preserving operations. When this set is restricted to the CZ gate together with preparation and measurement in the X basis, we show that the complexity of the required syndrome extraction gadgets essentially cancels the benefit of the noise bias: at experimentally relevant error rates, one may as well ignore the bias and rely on standard error correction designed for depolarizing noise. The situation changes drastically when a bias-preserving CX gate is available: the hierarchy of errors can then be reflected in the structure of the code, with frequent phase-flips corrected by a dedicated high-threshold code and rare bit-flips by concatenation with a high-rate code. The same hierarchy also enables hardware-efficient preparation of magic states. Finally, as a bias-preserving CX is forbidden in naturally biased platforms and challenging in engineered ones, we present a measurement-based architecture in which a high-fidelity quantum non-demolition readout of multi-qubit Pauli Z operators takes its place, extending these overhead reductions to a much broader range of physical platforms.

summary.summary: This review analyzes fault-tolerant protocols for biased-noise qubits where phase-flip errors vastly exceed bit-flip errors, examining three architectures based on available bias-preserving operations. The key finding is that substantial overhead reduction requires either a bias-preserving CX gate or high-fidelity quantum non-demolition readout of multi-qubit Pauli Z operators; with only CZ gates, the noise bias provides negligible practical benefit.
summary.motivation: Biased-noise qubits from natural (electron/nuclear spins) and engineered (cat qubits) platforms promise reduced overhead for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but this potential can only be realized if operations preserve rather than depolarize the noise bias.
summary.method: The review organizes prominent fault-tolerant architectures by their elementary bias-preserving gate sets: (1) {CZ, $\mathcal{P}_{|+\rangle}$, $\mathcal{M}_X$}, (2) {CZ, CX, CY, $\mathcal{P}_{|0\rangle}$, $\mathcal{P}_{|+\rangle}$, $\mathcal{M}_X$, $\mathcal{M}_Z$}, and (3) QND readout of $Z^{\otimes n}$ operators, with numerical analysis using circuit-level noise models at $p_Z = 10^{-3}$ per operation.
summary.result: With CZ only, a distance-9 surface code for depolarizing noise ($\approx 161$ qubits for $10^{-6}$ logical error rate) remains superior; with bias-preserving CX, concatenated repetition/high-rate codes achieve $< 8$ qubits per logical qubit at $\eta \gg 1$; unfolded distillation prepares $|X^{1/4}\rangle$ magic states with $\sim 10^{-8}$ logical error using 53 qubits at $p_Z = 10^{-3}$ with $\eta = 5\times10^7$.

papers.title: Microwave-driven same-species sympathetic cooling for trapped ions
papers.abstract: Sympathetic cooling of data qubits by coolant ions is an essential technique for trapped-ion quantum computing. Conventionally a second ion species is used, requiring additional lasers and complicating optical setups. We propose a scheme for sympathetic cooling using the same species and test it for $^{43}$Ca$^+$ ions. Pulsed sideband cooling and ion addressing are implemented via integrated microwave control, further simplifying optical requirements. We cool a two-ion gate mode close to its ground state ($\bar{n}\approx 0.16$) and benchmark an induced error on the data qubit of $1.7(4)\times 10^{-4}$ per cooling cycle.

summary.summary: This work demonstrates sympathetic cooling of trapped $^{43}$Ca$^+$ ions using same-species and same-isotope ions, with both data and coolant qubits encoded in the ground-state $4S_{1/2}$ manifold and addressed via microwave-driven pulsed sideband cooling. The scheme achieves ground-state cooling of a two-ion rocking mode to $\bar{n} \approx 0.16$ phonons with an induced error of $1.7(4) \times 10^{-4}$ per cooling cycle on the data qubit.
summary.motivation: Conventional sympathetic cooling uses a second ion species to avoid crosstalk, requiring additional laser infrastructure and complicating optical setups. Implementing same-isotope cooling with microwave control simplifies the experiment while enabling quantum-information preservation in clock-state qubits within the ground manifold.
summary.method: Data and coolant ions are separated in frequency using Zeeman splitting in a static magnetic field of 28.8 mT. Pulsed resolved-sideband cooling drives the $|3,2\rangle \to |4,2\rangle$ motional sideband at 2.908 GHz with compensation tones to cancel ac Zeeman shifts; cooling cycles are interleaved with spin-echo pulses on the data qubit ($|4,1\rangle$ to $|3,1\rangle$ at 3.123 GHz) to correct residual frequency drifts.
summary.result: After 16 cooling cycles, the in-plane radial rocking mode ($\omega = 2\pi \times 5.37$ MHz) is cooled from $1.7(2)$ quanta to $\bar{n} = 0.16(2)$ quanta at a rate of $0.27(1)$ quanta/cycle; the data qubit error is dominated by thermal drifts in the microwave drive chain at $1.2(3) \times 10^{-4}$ per cycle from the sideband pulse, with a fundamental limit from 393 nm photon scattering estimated at $1.6(9) \times 10^{-6}$ per cycle.
